faqs.q: Why are there so many squirrels in Kingston attics?
faqs.a: Our crew's Kingston work centers on Norway rats in Rondout and Midtown, raccoons along the creeks, and bats in the older Uptown homes. That is why we pair removal with proofing on every Kingston job rather than just taking the animal out.

Kingston.wildlife_intro:
Kingston keeps our crew busy with Norway rats in Rondout and Midtown, raccoons along the creeks, and bats in the older Uptown homes. Rondout Creek  gives wildlife food, water, and cover within a short run of almost every roof in town, and the housing does the rest — once an animal finds a soft soffit, an uncapped chimney, or a gap at the roofline, it treats the house as part of its territory.

The year has a rhythm in Kingston. Fall pushes squirrels, raccoons, and rodents indoors ahead of winter; spring brings denning mothers looking for chimneys and attic corners; summer is when bat colonies are most visible in older homes and when young animals start ranging on their own. Most Kingston jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in New Paltz?
faqs.a: New Paltz mixes owner-occupied village homes, student rentals, and rural properties, and the scope differs for each — rentals especially need the between-tenant inspection documented. We walk the property, identify the entries, and quote removal and sealing in writing.

faqs.q: I found a snake near my New Paltz home. Can you remove it?
faqs.a: New York treats every native snake as permit-gated: even a DEC-licensed Nuisance Wildlife Control Operator needs a special depredation permit to handle one, and the Shawangunk foothills around New Paltz include copperhead habitat — DEC documented one in the village in 2025. Keep your distance, keep pets away, and call us for identification and safety guidance; we will refer you to DEC or a specially permitted operator for any hands-on work.

New Paltz.wildlife_intro:
New Paltz sits between the Wallkill River's flats and the Shawangunk Ridge, a college village of stone houses on Huguenot Street, student rentals, orchards, and newer homes spreading toward the ridge. Skunks and squirrels generate the steady call volume — skunks under the porches of the older village homes, squirrels in the canopy attics — and the ridge's rocky woods bring a question most towns never ask: what kind of snake is in the garden?

That question has a careful answer in New Paltz, where DEC conservation officers have documented a copperhead in the village area. All native snakes in New York sit outside a standard operator's license, so our role with snakes is identification, safety guidance, and referral to a specially permitted operator or DEC — never handling. For everything else, our crew inspects New Paltz homes roof to porch, removes the animals, and seals the entries, with rental properties checked between tenants when problems usually surface.

faqs.q: What does it cost to get an animal out of my Saugerties attic?
faqs.a: Village homes and rural properties price apart in Saugerties: a compact village attic is one scope, a farmhouse with a barn is another. We inspect the property you have, show you the entries, and quote removal and sealing in writing — seasonal owners get photographs of everything.

faqs.q: What should seasonal owners in Saugerties check in spring?
faqs.a: Attics and chimneys first. A house closed from October to April on the Catskill edge is an open invitation, and raccoons and bats both take it; by spring there may be a litter or a returning colony in place. Our crew inspects before you settle in, removes any occupants through exclusion or trapping as the species requires, and seals the entries so next winter is quiet.

Saugerties.wildlife_intro:
Saugerties spreads from its Hudson riverfront village — lighthouse at the creek mouth, brick Main Street blocks, pre-war homes — out into Catskill-edge farm and forest country. Raccoons are the constant, commuting between Esopus Creek, the river shore, and the attics of both village homes and rural properties. Bats colonize the older village housing, and the rural roads add groundhogs, skunks, and seasonal camps where animals winter undisturbed.

The town's size means two service patterns: tight village inspections where houses share tree canopy and rooflines nearly touch, and rural property inspections where the barn matters as much as the house. Our crew handles Saugerties calls accordingly, removes the animals, and seals the dwelling — and for the many seasonal places toward the mountains, we check for the winter-long bat and raccoon occupancy that empty houses here reliably develop.

faqs.q: What should I expect to pay for wildlife removal in Ellenville?
faqs.a: Ellenville's compact older homes keep most attic jobs contained, but porch and shed screening is so often part of the real fix that we quote it in the same visit. We inspect, tell you plainly which voids are active, and give you a written figure for removal and screening together.

faqs.q: Why does Ellenville have so many skunks?
faqs.a: Porches, sheds, and short blocks: the village's housing gives striped skunks a den site every few houses, and the valley floor feeds them well. Skunks are a designated rabies-vector species in New York, so den evictions are professional work. Our crew removes the animals and screens the void perimeters — an unscreened porch in Ellenville is re-let within a season or two.

Ellenville.wildlife_intro:
Ellenville lies in the Rondout Valley between the Shawangunk Ridge and the Catskill foothills, a small village with a hard-working past — knife factories, canal and rail years, resort summers — and housing to match: compact older homes, doubles, and modest streets under the ridge. Skunks are the village's most-reported animal, denning under porches and sheds on nearly every block, with raccoons in the older attics and squirrels along the tree streets.

The ridge looming over Ellenville is real snake and denning habitat, but the daily work is porch-level: skunk families in June, raccoon litters in spring chimneys, and fall squirrels. Our crew inspects Ellenville homes completely, removes the animals, and screens the porch and shed voids that this village offers in unusual density — in Ellenville, sealing the roof without screening the porch solves the smaller half of most complaints.

faqs.q: How much will a wildlife job run in Woodstock?
faqs.a: Woodstock quotes turn on occupancy: a lived-in village home is a standard inspection, while a mountain-road second home may need entries documented and sealed across several structures. We inspect, photograph everything for owners who are away, and quote removal and sealing in writing.

faqs.q: What are flying squirrels, and are they in Woodstock attics?
faqs.a: They are small nocturnal squirrels native to New York's forests, and Woodstock's wooded lots are prime habitat — they enter through gaps as small as a coin at rooflines and gable vents, usually in colonies, and are active after dark when gray squirrels are not. Our crew confirms them from timing and droppings, removes them, and seals to the finer standard their size demands.

Woodstock.wildlife_intro:
Woodstock is the Catskills' famous arts colony: a village of galleries and old homes along the Tinker Street corridor, wrapped in forest, with second homes and seasonal rentals scattered up the mountain roads. That forest-and-empty-house combination defines its wildlife work — bats in the eaves of cabins and colonials left quiet for weeks, raccoons in chimneys of weekend homes, and flying squirrels, the Catskill specialty, gliding into attics from the surrounding woods.

Undetected time is the enemy in Woodstock: a colony or litter can be established for a month before an owner returns. Our crew inspects Woodstock properties with that in mind, photographs every entry for absentee owners, removes the animals, and seals thoroughly — flying squirrels need gaps closed that gray squirrels could never use, so the sealing standard on a forest-edge house is finer than in the suburbs.
